## 2. Agent-routing replay (prequential: route, then reveal the label, then feedback; same order for all)
Candidates = the fr-* agents. Reward = 1 if the pick equals actual_agent, else 0. Report the label's limitation: it is "what the leader chose", not ground-truth optimality.
Routers:
a) ruflo keyword: CLI `node C:[REDACTED:high_entropy]@claude-flow/cli/bin/cli.js hooks route --task "<text>"` (map its suggested agent to the nearest fr-* role, and document the mapping). If it is too slow per call, sample and say so.

d) a trivial baseline: "pipeline-phase rule" (planner → builder/tester → reviewer → scriber → shipper by phase keyword). This is what the project's CLAUDE.md effectively does today.
Metrics: overall accuracy, accuracy on the last half (after learning), number of rows before each learner first matches the rule baseline, and per-agent confusion.

## 3. Model-tier / token check with @metaharness/router (now installed)
Use ruflo's neural router with env CLAUDE_FLOW_ROUTER_NEURAL=1, CLAUDE_FLOW_ROUTER_SEED_CORPUS and CLAUDE_FLOW_ROUTER_MODEL_PATH = C:/Users/mariu/.claude/plugins/marketplaces/ruflo/v3/@claude-flow/cli/assets/model-router/{seed-rows.json,seed-router.krr.json}. If you cannot produce a matching embedding, say so and use routeToModelFull's heuristic path, labelled as such. For each dataset row, record the suggested model, routedBy, and confidence.
Then compare against actual_model and the measured tokens. Compute an ESTIMATED cost delta: the tokens that actually ran, priced at the router's suggested model vs the actual model. Use the published per-MTok prices in ruflo's own model table (cite the file). Label it clearly as an estimate: switching model does not reduce tokens, and a cheaper model may fail and need re-runs. Also check the outcomes: would the router have sent any phase that needed fix rounds to a cheaper tier?

## 4. Context to include from the repos' own evidence (already run today: hebbian-router 42/42 tests, experiment reproduced; neural-mesh lib 403/403)
Summarise in 3-5 lines: hebbian-router README conclusion (Hebbian ≈ Thompson; the mesh-style no-decay rule is clearly worse, 0.518) and neural-mesh RD-LOG.md FINAL ROUNDUP (kNN router + OOD abstain −58..−70% forwarded tokens on novel phrasing; "tool routes would have saved ~0 tokens on real delegated agent traffic", R88). Also check whether neural-mesh's route CLI uses the decay/baseline rule or the no-decay mesh.rs rule (read src/hebbian.rs and src/mesh.rs). That decides whether the hebbian-router warning applies to it.

## Output
Write router-eval/REPORT.md with tables, the exact commands, row counts, seeds, and every assumption labelled. Keep the scripts in router-eval/ so they can be re-run. Return a concise verdict (≤ 25 lines), one per router: (1) more accurate than the rule baseline on our data or not, (2) needs more training (is the learning curve still rising? how many more labelled rows would plausibly be needed?), (3) measured or estimated token/cost effect, clearly marked. The router comparison on this project's real history is done. None of the routers beats the simple keyword rule yet, and the learning ones need more training data.

**Agent choice** (69 real dispatches, replayed in order):

| Router | Accuracy (overall / last half) |
|---|---|
| Keyword rule (only the 6 phase verbs) | 72.5% / 80.0% |
| neural-mesh, told the right answer after each task | 67.3% / 74.3% |
| Hebbian, told the right answer | 63.2% |
| ruflo `hooks route` | 30.4% (47.8% with its MiniLM embedder) |
| neural-mesh / Hebbian, success-or-fail feedback only | 33% / 28% |

- The "right answer" is just which agent the leader actually picked, not proof it was the best choice.
- **More training needed: yes.** neural-mesh's accuracy is still rising across the stream (51% → 72% → 78% by thirds).
- **But repetition won't fix it.** On task wording it hasn't seen, Hebbian stalls at about 68%, so they need more *different* labelled tasks, not more passes over the same ones.
- **Tokens:** choosing agents doesn't use LLM tokens, so a better agent router saves none. The real waste in this data was re-dispatches (18% of all tokens, from blocked worktrees, turn limits and a rate limit) plus fix rounds (15%).

**Model tier (`@metaharness/router`, now running on the real neural path):**
- Our tasks look nothing like its training examples, and its predicted quality was below its own bar on every task.
- It would cut cost by roughly 46–77%, but that only re-prices the same tokens at a cheaper model. A cheaper model could fail and need re-runs.
- It would have sent 15–16 of the 20 phases that later had defects or fix rounds to a cheaper model.
- **My recommendation:** keep it installed so it can be retrained on our own outcomes, but don't follow its picks yet. I can turn `CLAUDE_FLOW_ROUTER_NEURAL` off if you'd rather.
- One correction to my earlier note: neural-mesh's `route` command uses the decay-and-baseline rule, so the "no-decay rule is clearly worse" warning doesn't apply to it.

**Effect on the hive:** I've shared these results on the hive board. The phase 2 plan now targets what this data shows actually wastes tokens:
- Learning from labelled agent outcomes
- Generalising to new wording (similar tasks share what was learned)
- Spotting phases likely to need fix rounds before they go to a cheaper model

Subagents in this setup can't write report files, so the four hive agents will send their findings back to me and I'll post them on the board. The report is saved at `scratchpad/router-eval/REPORT.md`.

I put seven agents to work, read everything they found, and had a devil's-advocate agent attack my first draft. The critique changed the answer.

**Short version:** don't try to be the company that collects detention money. Be the software that makes detention claims hard to deny, and sell it to the companies that already legally own the money: factoring companies and mid-size brokers. Small carriers get a free tool that feeds the system with data.

## What the research established

- **The prize is smaller than the pitch.** The recoverable pool is about **$3.6B a year** of direct, unreimbursed US detention. ATRI's $15.1B is mostly lost productivity. [A]
- **Where the money is lost:**
  - Carriers invoice about 75% of detention events, and about 55% of those invoices get paid, so only about **41%** of events are paid at all. [A]
  - Claims die before any dispute starts: there's no detention clause in the rate confirmation, the 24–72 hour notice window is missed, or the only timestamp is the driver's word. [B]
- **What wins:** the contract clause, two independent timestamps (the signed in/out time on the BOL is the industry standard second one), notice sent at the time of the wait, and an invoice sent inside the deadline. [B]
- **The choke point:** about two-thirds of brokers only pay detention if they can collect it from the shipper. [B]
- **The gap:**
  - Telematics apps (DockClock, FleetOptos, GeoStamp, Motive) detect detention, each tied to one ELD brand.
  - Loop ($95M) audits invoices for large shippers on subscription.
  - Factoring companies fund invoices but don't fight the disputes.
  - **Nobody takes a claim from detection all the way to an enforceable claim, a dispute and collection.** [B]
- **Europe isn't the place to start.** Germany has a statutory right to waiting-time pay (Standgeld), but Norway's rights are contract-only. The verdict is US-first, with Germany as the first European test. [~55% confidence]

## The critique that changed my plan

1. **A carrier-only contingency business probably doesn't pay.** A 20-truck carrier is worth roughly **$4K a year** in fees, so any human support per account wipes out the margin. The financial model was built for shippers and never modelled carriers.
2. **Factoring makes the money someone else's.** Most small carriers sell their invoices, so the factoring company owns the detention receivable and controls collection. A contingency fee would set three parties against each other.
3. **Legal exposure.** Chasing other firms' receivables for a percentage can count as licensed debt collection in some US states. Demand letters and suggested contract language sold for a fee raise unauthorized-practice-of-law questions.
4. **Broker AP doesn't work the way I assumed.** Accounts-payable teams match invoices inside their own TMS; they don't open third-party links. A public "verify" page would also leak confidential rates.

## The refined strategy

**Positioning: "Detention you can't argue with."** We're the evidence and enforcement software, not the collector.

1. **Free clause check for carriers (the wedge).** A carrier forwards a rate confirmation by email and gets back: missing or weak detention clause, notice deadline, rate cap, and attorney-reviewed clause language. The critic rated this the strongest idea:
   - it needs no ELD integration;
   - it involves no collection, so no licensing risk;
   - onboarding is nearly zero-touch;
   - it stops the biggest claim-killer before any money is at stake;
   - it builds a dataset of rate confirmations nobody else has.
2. **The paying customers are factoring companies and mid-size brokers.** Both already own the receivable and have the right to contact the payer, so we sell them software (subscription plus a success fee) instead of collecting ourselves.
   - Factoring companies get a white-label tool that recovers detention across thousands of carriers.
   - Brokers get help collecting from shippers, which is exactly their choke point.
3. **Evidence that's hard to deny.**
   - Read the signed in/out times off the BOL and pair them with ELD geofence times.
   - Quote the contract clause.
   - Export a signed PDF that the recipient can verify offline. No public links.
   - All of this reuses what's already built: the audit chain, four-eyes approvals and field-level provenance.
4. **Payer scores built from real outcomes.** Which brokers and shippers actually pay, and how fast. For factoring companies this feeds straight into their credit scoring, which is a reason for them to stay. It needs an outcome ledger first.
5. **Later:** a "defence" product for shippers (catching detention billed inside free time, or billed twice by broker and carrier), and Germany.

**Don't:**
- blockchain;
- generic tracking;
- building voice agents (partner instead);
- guarantees or financing;
- Norway first;
- scraping customer portals;
- citing $15.1B or Nuvocargo's unsourced $47K.

## What to do next (mostly not code)

1. **Remove section A.4 of `business/investor-brief.md`.** It claims a Hebbian router, "250x" and "smarter with every claim", and none of that exists in the product. It has to go before any investor sees the brief.
2. **Build a unit-economics model for carriers, factoring companies and brokers,** with a numeric kill line, for example "under $15K a year recoverable per paying account means stop".
3. **Get a 1–2 hour opinion from a US freight or collections attorney** on licensing, demand letters and sending notices on someone else's behalf.
4. **Read 3 factoring agreements:** who owns accessorial charges, and who may contact the payer.
5. **Run interviews:** 3 factoring companies, 3 mid-size brokers and 10 carriers. Ask each carrier which ELD they use; Samsara may not fit small fleets, and Motive might.
6. **Clause-check test:** collect about 20 rate confirmations from each of 10 carriers and count the missing or weak clauses. Do this *by hand, outside the product*: CLAUDE.md's synthetic-data rule still holds until the security sign-off.
7. **Get a US advisor or design partner from inside a factoring company or carrier group.** A solo founder in Norway needs US presence, insurance and coverage during US hours.

**Engineering, once validated:**
1. Port the rules engine to the TypeScript platform.
2. Add an outcome ledger.
3. Add a closed-file audit mode.
4. Build a real test set.
5. Add rate-confirmation clause extraction and BOL time extraction with provenance.
6. Add the signed packet PDF.

Plugin help along the way:
- **BM25 clause search:** neural-mesh's measured winner, rebuilt in TypeScript.
- **Signed evaluation receipts:** `eval-conductor`.
- **Packet PDFs:** self-hosted Carbone.
- **Geofences:** PostGIS.

**Confidence:**
- High on the market numbers and the gap.
- Medium on factoring companies and brokers as the paying customers: that's the critic's argument plus mine, not yet tested.
- Low on the legal questions and on Europe until the attorney and the primary texts are checked.

In short: the platform saves money mainly by billing detention that never gets invoiced today. It can improve over time without model training, but the biggest money assumption still needs real outcome data from pilots.

## Data I found and used

| Data | Type | How I used it |
|---|---|---|
| Rules tariffs from 4 carriers: Dohrn 2025, Magnum 2026, Gardewine 2025, States Logistics 2023 | **Real** | 103 billable charge names, copied word for word, as a test set |
| [ATRI 2024 detention study](https://truckingresearch.[REDACTED:high_entropy].pdf) | Real survey of 587 drivers and 245 carriers | How often detention happens, how long it lasts, hourly rates, and how often it is billed and paid |
| [FMCSA](https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/research-and-analysis/impact-driver-detention-time-safety-and-operations), [DOT OIG 2018](https://www.oversight.gov/reports/audit/estimates-show-commercial-driver-detention-increases-crash-risks-and-costs-current), [OOIDA 2023](https://www.ooida.[REDACTED:high_entropy].pdf) | Real | Cross-checks on the ATRI numbers |
| [XPO tariff](https://www.xpo.com/cdn/download_files/s1/p2831/CNWY_199-AJ.4_Eff_11.3.2025.pdf), [J.B. Hunt standard accessorials](https://www.jbhunt.com/blog/2020/12/11/standardized-accessorials-in-carrier-360) | Real contract terms | Free time, hourly rates and caps |
| [USAID SCMS](https://data.amerigeoss.org/dataset/supply-chain-shipment-pricing-data), [Olist](https://github.com/olist/work-at-olist-data), [BTS CFS](https://data.transportation.gov/) | Real shipment-level data | Found but not used. They have no detention or invoice lines, and Olist is parcel deliveries, not truckloads |

Nobody publishes a real dataset of freight invoice lines. My own synthetic data appears only where nothing real exists: the charge wordings in test 2, and the detention events in test 3, which are random draws shaped by ATRI's survey numbers. The real data is in `%TEMP%\realdata`, outside the repo; hard rule 4 still governs what goes into the repo.

## Does it save money?

**Test 1: simulation of 1,000 truckload shipments,** with ATRI's numbers driving the random draws. The detention amounts came from the platform's own calculation engine.

| Scenario | Collected per 1,000 loads | Extra vs today |
|---|---|---|
| Detention owed | $56,400 | |
| Collected today (bill rate × pay rate) | $22,600 (40%) | |
| Platform bills every event that has gate times; brokers pay as often as now | $30,200 | **+$7,500** |
| Evidence packets raise the paid rate to 65% | $35,300 | **+$12,700** |
| Paid rate rises to 75% | $40,300 | **+$17,700** |
| Only 60% of loads have usable gate times | $27,600 | **+$5,100** |

The model's 40% collected today matches ATRI's independent 36–46%, a good check that it's calibrated. A 50-truck carrier runs about 5,000 loads a year, so that's roughly **$25k–90k a year** in extra detention collected.

**The biggest lever is unmeasured:** whether evidence packets make brokers actually pay more often. No public data covers that, so only pilot outcomes can answer it. Gate-time coverage matters almost as much.

On invoice auditing, only vendor claims exist: 3–6% of invoices contain errors and 1–5% of freight spend is recoverable. I found no independent study, so treat those numbers as weak.

## Can it improve over time? Does it need training?

The money maths should never learn. It stays deterministic and auditable. Learning pays off in reading the documents, and I measured that with ruvector:

**Test 2: sorting invoice charge lines into types.** The engine checks a charge against the rate confirmation only if it recognises the line as an accessorial.

| Test set | Keyword rules today | Nearest-match on labelled examples (ruvector embeddings) |
|---|---|---|
| **Real** charge names, labelled on 3 carriers and tested on the 4th | **11 of 93** accessorials recognised (12%) | **92 of 93** (99%); detention and fuel lines still 100% |
| Synthetic wordings I wrote, 168 labels | 28.6% | Accuracy rises as labels are added: 48% → 61% → 77% → **93%** |

The real-tariff result means that today most real accessorial charges are never checked for authorization, so overcharges go unflagged. One caveat on reading it: 90% of that set is accessorials, so look at recognition of accessorials rather than overall accuracy.

**What "training" means here:** no GPU and no model training. The system keeps a growing memory of labelled examples, and every reviewer correction helps the next invoice straight away. Correction data is already being collected: the review screens record every field correction.

**Data it needs:**
- **Available now:** charge-line labels, starting with the 103 real tariff names I collected.
- **Pilots only:** paid and denied outcomes. They decide the paid-rate question above and enable "which brokers pay" insights.

**Next step I'd suggest:** a learned charge-line classifier inside the platform. The rules stay in charge of the money; the classifier suggests line types from the tariff names plus reviewer corrections, and a person confirms. Say the word and I'll plan it through the same build/test/review process as Step 5.

I've also saved this study to project memory. The scripts are in `%TEMP%\clf`.

## Research findings

**Customers:**
- **Mid-size shippers and importers come first:** they have the most money at stake and are used to paying recovery fees.
- **Brokers next:** they run on about 15% gross margins and absorb accessorials when they can't re-bill them.
- **Carriers last, through partners such as factoring companies:** their operating margins are around −2% to +0.4%, and detention is paid on fewer than half of invoices.

**Can we predict prices?** I tested this on real public data, scoring each forecast only on what happened after it was made:

| Prediction | Result vs "price stays the same" |
|---|---|
| Diesel, 1 week ahead | **15% better** (statistically clear) |
| Diesel, 4 weeks ahead | 4% better (real but small) |
| Diesel, 8–13 weeks; ocean freight; lane-level truck rates (78,824 forecasts) | **No edge.** This matches MIT research; DAT, SONAR and the other big rate vendors don't publish any comparison against this baseline. |
| "80%" price ranges | The usual method covered only 62–76% of outcomes. My volatility-scaled method covers **74–81%**. |

**Cheaper cargo ships:** not a fit. Our customers book container space rather than chartering ships, the index data needs paid licences, and no forecasting edge has been shown. What does fit is **container demurrage and detention (D&D) fees**. US rules make a non-compliant invoice legally unpayable.

The business case is in `business/business-case-2026-10-cost-intelligence.md`, with every number graded and linked to its source.

## What was built

**Step 7: fuel-surcharge check and cost outlook**
- **Fuel check:** recomputes each fuel surcharge from the official weekly diesel price and the customer's own surcharge table, and flags billing with the wrong week. Example: a $435 surcharge on a $420 shipment is flagged as $15 over.
- **Price data:** public diesel and truckload price history is bundled with the app, with a safe importer for updates.
- **Outlook:** shows forecasts only where the backtest proved an edge, and switches each one back to "no change" automatically if the edge disappears.

**Step 8: ocean D&D invoice audit**
- **Legal checks:** required invoice items, the 30-day billing deadline, dispute windows, and fees charged while a container was unavailable or its empty return was refused.
- **Tariff maths:** checked against real Maersk, MSC, Hapag-Lloyd and CMA CGM tariffs. For example, 15 days past free time on a Maersk 40-foot box is $3,910.
- **Output:** a draft dispute letter that quotes the regulation.

**Quality:** both steps went through spec, build, separate tests, security review and final review. Findings that were fixed:
- Step 7: two Low items (re-imports that silently change past prices; untraceable fuel-table edits) and a missing API-key test.
- Step 8: a Medium memory issue in the invoice list, and the four-eyes gap below.
- Light tests on Node 22 pass: Step 7 has 263 shared and 20 API tests; Step 8 has 393 shared, 12 API and 32 web tests.

- 46 CFR 541.4 ("who may be billed") was struck down by a federal appeals court in September 2025, so the product doesn't check it.

I ran the full test suites and evaluated the waiting candidate model. It does not get promoted, and the evaluation turned up two real bugs, both now fixed and committed locally in `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh`.

**Bugs fixed:**
1. **The nightly evaluation crashed every night.** Its code test questions had no precomputed answers to check against, so the trained model was never tested. They're now computed at load time, the same way the benchmark generator does it, and match its file exactly (commit `45621db`).
2. **The fixed test battery could never fail.** Its scorer returns a result record, but the code treated any non-empty record as "correct", so every answer passed. The check that blocks a model which got worse could never fire. It now uses the real right/wrong verdict and stops the evaluation if the code-test sandbox errors (commit `43f5a07`). Seven new tests cover both fixes, including one that runs the real scorer on a wrong answer.

**Candidate model** (trained on 277 examples from your sessions, compared with the plain base model, which is still production):

| Test | Base model | Candidate | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Held-out loss (perplexity) | 20.4 | 14.6 | Better, statistically clear |
| Pairwise judge, 60 questions both orders | | 27 wins, 10 ties, 23 losses | 53% win rate, CI 42–64%: not a significant win |
| Math, 20 questions | 8 | 3 | Worse |
| Physics, 20 questions | 8 | 1 | Worse |
| Research, 20 questions | 9 | 6 | Worse |
| Code, 20 questions | 18 | 17 | About the same |

**Verdict: keep production.** The candidate has learned to imitate your sessions' style, but it has lost general reasoning ability. Bug 2 mattered: under the old scoring, a future candidate that won the pairwise test would have been promoted despite these regressions. No damage was done, because nothing has ever been promoted. The judge cost $0.58, and the re-run reused cached answers at no extra cost.

**Tests:**

| Suite | Result |
